About me

I'm Yetu Silva. Becoming an engineer was always my goal, and I achieved it when I completed my integrated master's at the University of Southampton.

Now I'm ready for the next step. I want to bring the knowledge and hard work from my degree into a professional engineering career. During my degree I worked on power networks and control systems. I also explored wireless communications and AI tools. What I enjoy most is turning a technical problem into a design that works in practice.

I was born in Angola and moved to the UK during the Covid pandemic. I came with one clear aim, which was to build my career on the international stage. Living and studying in another country has broadened the way I think about engineering. That is why I want to carry this perspective forward and use it on projects around the world.

Away from engineering, I lead basketball training as Sports Officer for the University of Southampton African and Caribbean Society.

Projects

Smart meter power supply and case

Team design project, 2023 to 2024

Our team built a smart meter, a device that measures how much electricity a home uses. I was responsible for its power supply with one teammate. I also helped design the 3D-printed case that holds it.

  • Simulated the power supply on a computer before building it, and set it to run at 50 Hz, the frequency of UK mains electricity.
  • Designed it to turn mains electricity into a steady 12 V supply, delivering 6.63 A in simulation. It first converts alternating current into direct current, then smooths it and holds the voltage steady. I then built it by hand on a circuit board.
  • Co-designed the snap-together case in Fusion 360, a 3D design program. It had to keep water out, so it has a clear cover over the screen and a seat for a rubber seal. We also had to weigh up how screw holes could weaken that seal.

Multisim, Fusion 360, 3D printing, circuit building

Smart surfaces that redirect wireless signals

Individual final-year project, 2025, supervised by Prof. Mohammed El-Hajjar

When a building blocks a phone signal, the connection gets weak. A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) is a panel of small tiles that can each be tuned to send a reflected radio signal in a chosen direction. This way the walls around us can help a signal get past obstacles, which matters for 5G and future 6G networks.

I built a computer simulation in MATLAB to compare three ways of connecting these tiles. For each one, I measured how many errors reached the receiver and how much data the link could carry.

  • Compared tiles that work alone (diagonal), tiles linked in pairs along each row (non-diagonal), and tiles all linked together (fully-connected).
  • Tested each design with one transmitting antenna and then with several. I added realistic background noise and the fading you get in busy cities.
  • Found that the non-diagonal design comes close to the best performance in some cases at much lower cost. The diagonal design remains the simplest and cheapest to build.

Power network design and protection

Power Systems coursework, 2024 to 2025

I designed a model of a regional power network in PowerFactory, a professional tool for simulating power grids. The network brings electricity in at 132,000 volts and steps it down to 11,000 volts for four local areas. I chose the size of its cables, transformers and generator. Then I tested how it behaves in normal use and when equipment fails. Pick a scenario to see what happened.

  • Compared two layouts. In a ring, each area can be supplied by more than one route. In a radial layout, each area has a single supply line.
  • Found that if transformer T2 fails, T1 must carry 138.4% of its rated load. That is above its 120% short-term limit, so the design needs a larger transformer.
  • Chose protection devices that detect a fault and quickly switch off only the damaged section, so the rest of the network stays powered.

PowerFactory, power flow studies, fault analysis

BloctoGPT, an AI assistant for blockchain tools

Group design project with industry partner Bloctopus, 2025 to 2026

AI assistants can use outside tools to get tasks done, but they make more mistakes when there are too many tools to choose from. Our team built BloctoGPT with the blockchain company Bloctopus to solve this. It splits a request into smaller tasks. It then finds the tools that matter and bundles them into a few groups, so the AI only chooses from a short list.

  • I focused on research, testing and fixing bugs, and made sure our build reflected what we learned from published research.
  • In the later stages I co-led the part that teaches the system which tools match which requests.
  • Wrote up our design decisions for technical review in a team of four from different backgrounds.

Coaxial cable analysis

Transmission lines lab, 2024

Coaxial cable is the round cable used for TV aerials and internet connections. A copper wire runs through the centre, surrounded by insulation and a metal shield. I worked out the cable's key electrical properties from its size alone. Then I checked my results against a detailed computer simulation.

  • The inner wire has a radius of 0.58 mm and the shield a radius of 3.7 mm.
  • Calculated how the cable stores energy in its magnetic and electric fields along each metre of its length.
  • Found an impedance of about 74 Ω, close to the 75 Ω standard for TV cable. Impedance decides how cleanly a cable passes signals to the equipment at each end. Signals travel through it at about two-thirds of the speed of light.

Microchip design

Team of six, 2023 to 2024

Our team designed a microchip that was then manufactured. I designed the circuit that spots a specific 9-bit pattern in incoming data. Then I helped test the finished chip against our computer model.

Digital filter on a programmable chip

Digital design lab, 2023 to 2024

Built a digital filter that removes unwanted frequencies from a signal. It runs on an FPGA, a chip that can be programmed to act as custom hardware. I made the design adjustable for different signal sizes and added a filter that cuts out one narrow frequency. I tested it in simulation before loading it onto the chip.

Grouping words with machine learning

Machine Learning Technologies, 2024

Wrote a Python program that cleans up a large text, then sorts its words into groups based on how they appear together. I tested different numbers of groups and chose three, the simplest option that still separated the words well.
